pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Fluently add and subtract within 10 — quick, accurate, flexible recall of all facts to 10. A high-centrality fluency hub (0.17); automaticity here frees working memory for the making-ten strategy and all larger calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20 (facts within 10 the core subset); Y2 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 'add and subtract within 20… demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10'.
• Operational details — Extend within-5 fluency using derived-fact strategies: bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1. Push from counting toward recall via the ten-frame image and known-fact reasoning, then consolidate with short frequent retrieval practice. Include all subtraction facts and link them to their addition partners (fact families). Fluency = efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): answer within-10 additions using a fast strategy (bonds, doubles) rather than counting all. Tier B (age 6-7): recall any within-10 fact quickly and give its related subtraction. Tier C (age 7): use within-10 facts fluently to reason about larger calculations (e.g. 6+7 via 6+6+1).
bestPractices: Anchor fluency in derived-fact strategies (bonds to 10, doubles/near-doubles, +0/+1) so facts are recalled meaningfully and reconstructable if forgotten.
Use the ten-frame image and rekenrek to move children from counting to 'seeing' facts, then fade the support.
Teach addition and subtraction as fact families (6+4=10, 10−4=6) so subtraction facts come from known additions.
Consolidate with short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval rather than long timed tests; interleave facts so children discriminate rather than pattern-guess.
Model choosing an efficient strategy for each fact (flexibility), not one method for all.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) for facts and complements within 10
Rekenrek (two rows of 5) for doubles and bridging
Doubles/near-doubles visual (two equal rows, one extra)
Fact-family triangle linking a bond's + and − facts
Quick-image flash cards for retrieval practice
commonMisconceptions: Persisting with count-all/count-on for every fact instead of using derived facts or recall.
Mastering additions but not the related subtractions within 10.
Treating fluency as pure speed, leading to errors under pressure or anxiety.
Not recognising doubles/near-doubles as a shortcut (computing 6+7 from scratch).
Confusing similar facts (7+2 vs 7+3) when practice isn't interleaved.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, build fluent (efficient, accurate, flexible) addition and subtraction within 10, moving children from counting toward recall and derived-fact reasoning (bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1). Anchor facts in strategies so a forgotten fact can be reconstructed, link each addition to its subtraction partner as fact families, and consolidate with short, frequent, interleaved retrieval. The primary proposal is adaptive strategy-anchored retrieval practice with fading visual support; a fixed quiz, a static strategy anchor, and oral quick-fire are preserved as complementary tools with different purposes.

activities.title: Adaptive fluency practice with fading ten-frame support
feedback: If the child counts on each item, do not drill for speed under pressure or penalise counting; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and point to the known bond or double behind the fact — with continued short, frequent practice, automaticity typically develops.
If the child counts up from the smaller addend (e.g. 2 + 7 counted 3,4,5,6,7,8,9), prompt 'start from the bigger number' — this is an efficiency habit (commutativity), not a missing fact.
If complements to ten are slow (10 − 6 counted), pause and re-secure number bonds to 10 to automaticity; the rest of within-10 may already be fine.
When a fact is answered instantly, let the supporting image fade further so the child notices they now 'just know' it.
activities.rationale: Brief, low-pressure, strategy-anchored retrieval with fading support and interleaving is a key route to building meaningful automaticity; adaptivity lets support fade as recall strengthens and surfaces strategy hints when a child stalls.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency within 10, using strategies such as making ten, decomposing, and relationships between + and −.
learnerActions: Answer within-10 facts presented one after another (e.g. 6 + 4, 7 + 2, 9 − 4, 10 − 6), aiming to say the answer without counting.
Start with a faint ten-frame (or rekenrek image) behind each fact; as the child answers quickly, let the visual fade so they move from 'seeing' to recalling.
When a child stalls on a harder fact like 4 + 5, surface a strategy hint that shows the near-double (4 + 4 and one more) so they reconstruct rather than freeze.
Use a fact-family mode that surfaces the related subtraction for each bond (6 + 4 = 10 alongside 10 − 4 = 6, 10 − 6 = 4).
Interleave fact types (doubles, bonds, near-doubles, +/−1) so the child discriminates between similar facts (7 + 2 vs 7 + 3) rather than pattern-guesses.
activities.intendedInsight: A hard fact becomes easy when the child sees the double or bond inside it; isolated answers become a connected, flexible web of facts, including the subtraction partners — real fluency, not brittle speed.

activities.title: Interleaved fact quiz as a periodic check
feedback: Use results to spot which specific facts are still being counted and revisit the strategy behind them.
Favour short frequent sets over long timed tests, which can trigger errors or anxiety; fluency means efficient, accurate and flexible, not speed alone.
activities.rationale: Speeded retrieval practice drives automaticity, so fact quizzes are a legitimate practice and assessment tool; a fixed quiz is less adaptive than guided practice and is best used as a periodic check rather than the main teaching driver.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Work short sets of within-10 fact items (multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank), kept low-stakes and quick.
Include related-subtraction pairs alongside additions (e.g. 6 + 4 and 10 − 6) so both are practised.
Interleave fact types within a set rather than grouping all doubles or all bonds together.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick retrieval across mixed facts shows which facts are recalled versus still counted, and keeps subtraction facts practised alongside their addition partners.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up
feedback: Watch for recall versus counting on; the 10 − 6 item checks whether ten-facts are automatic (or whether the child counts back or counts up from 6), and the 7 + 2 item shows whether the child counts on from the larger addend.
Treat an exposed gap (e.g. ten-bonds not automatic) as the next thing to re-secure, not a reason to drill under time pressure.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire builds recall and makes reasoning audible; on its own it cannot deliver the volume of varied, adaptive repetition that written/adaptive practice provides, so it works best as a short warm-up.
learnerActions: Run a brief spoken quick-fire round of within-10 facts as a warm-up, e.g. '6 + 3? … 9 − 4? … 7 + 2? … 10 − 6?'

After an answer, ask follow-up questions: 'For 2 + 7, could you start from the 7 instead? Is it quicker?', 'How does knowing 6 + 4 = 10 help with 10 − 6?', 'Which did you just know without working out?', 'What's 9 − 4 — and how did you get it?'
activities.intendedInsight: Speaking facts aloud and explaining the strategy makes the child's recall-versus-counting visible and reinforces commutativity and fact-family links.

activities.title: Strategy reference anchor for derived facts
feedback: Use the anchor to prompt reconstruction, then return to retrieval so the child practises recalling without it.
Recognising a strategy on a wall is a scaffold; it does not by itself build the repeated retrieval that automaticity needs.
activities.rationale: A static strategy anchor aids recognition and reconstruction of facts but cannot drive repeated retrieval, so it supports rather than replaces active practice.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Keep a visible reference wall or card of key derived facts and strategies: doubles (two equal rows), near-doubles (one extra), bonds to 10 on a ten-frame, and fact-family triangles linking a bond's + and − facts.
Point to the matching strategy when a fact is forgotten so the child reconstructs it (e.g. find 4 + 5 via 4 + 4 and one more).
activities.intendedInsight: Having the underlying strategies visible helps children recognise and reconstruct facts meaningfully instead of guessing.

constraints: Fluency means efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone; avoid long timed tests that cause errors or anxiety and use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval instead.
Do not penalise counting under time pressure; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and derived-fact reasoning so automaticity develops naturally.
Include all subtraction facts within 10 and link them to their addition partners (fact families); mastering additions alone is incomplete.
Interleave fact types so children discriminate between similar facts rather than pattern-guess.
A static strategy anchor and an oral quick-fire are recognition/warm-up scaffolds; they do not by themselves deliver the repeated varied retrieval needed for automaticity.
Visual supports (ten-frame, rekenrek) should be faded as recall strengthens, not relied on permanently.
Number bonds to 10 are a prerequisite thread; if complements to ten are not automatic, re-secure number bonds to 10 rather than drilling all facts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed non-adaptive and static media as 'impossible' or unable to drive fluency; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (a quiz and a reference anchor can support learning but are less adaptive and cannot alone supply repeated retrieval). Catalog fit rankings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.
Source CCSS-M (1.OA.6) and the NCETM/retrieval-practice claim are marked verified:false in the legacy row; do not treat them as independently confirmed.

CCSS 1.OA.6 supports only the strategy/relationships element of activity 1; the speeded-retrieval, fading-support and interleaving mechanism rests on the NCETM claim, not on the CCSS standard statement.
Checkpoint answers in the source ('9, 5, 9, 4' for 6+3, 9−4, 7+2, 10−6) are correct: 6+3=9, 9−4=5, 7+2=9, 10−6=4.

The legacy claim that small-fact fluency 'is not spatial' (used to skip 3D) is a design preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is retained only as a reason to prioritise other media, not as a universal rule.

The DfE 'recall and use fluently' claim supports the objective/standard but not the specific retrieval-mechanism rationale, so it was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims and is represented at summary/objective level instead.
The raw prerequisite micro-topic identifier was stripped from learner-facing constraints; the number-bonds-to-10 prerequisite relationship is retained conceptually.

probeDeeper: For 2 + 7, could you start from the 7 instead? Is it quicker?
Which did you just know without working out?
What's 9 − 4 — and how did you get it?
assess.correctAnswer: 9, 5, 9, 4 — from memory or instant derivation, including the bond-to-ten 10 − 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on from the first addend or from one, rather than recalling within-10 facts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill for speed under pressure or penalise counting — model count-on-from-larger and use known bonds; automaticity follows naturally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Nodding / finger counting on each item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on from the SMALLER addend — does not use commutativity, so 2 + 7 is counted 3,4,5,6,7,8,9.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach 'start from the bigger number' (commutativity) — this is an efficiency habit, not a missing fact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child starts the count from the smaller number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bonds to 10 not automatic, dragging down 10 − facts — 10 − 6 is counted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-secure number bonds to 10 to automaticity; the rest of within-10 is fine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Struggles specifically on complements to ten.

responseLevels.gap: Counts on/all by ones for most facts; ten-bonds not automatic.
responseLevels.full: Recalls within-10 facts, including complements to ten, quickly and accurately, using commutativity to be efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls or derives most facts but still counts some, or starts counts from the smaller addend.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: As fast as you can, no counting: 6 + 3? … 9 − 4? … 7 + 2? … 10 − 6?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch recall versus counting on. Within-10 fluency should not need finger-counting; the 10 − 6 item checks whether ten-facts are automatic, and whether the child counts on from the larger number rather than re-counting.
